title: Extreme poverty in India halved to 2.6% in 2023 from year ago: World Bank data
where: Front page, continued on page 2 (Siddharth Upasani)
syllabus: GS1 › Poverty and developmental issues; Role of women · GS2 › Issues relating to poverty and hunger · GS3 › Inclusive growth; Employment · GS2 › International institutions (World Bank)
summary: The World Bank's Poverty & Equity Brief puts India's extreme poverty ($3 a day, 2021 PPP) at 2.6% in 2023, but flags wage gaps, regional concentration and low-productivity jobs.
ideas: Fast fall, on every line: extreme poverty fell from 27.1% (2011) to 5.3% (2022-23) and 2.6% (2023); the lower-middle-income line ($4.2) fell from 57.7% to 16.1%, lifting about 496 million people.
GS1 · Poverty
India recorded one of the world's fastest poverty declines, in monetary and non-monetary terms, says the World Bank.
Poverty is now a place, not just a condition: about 57% of India's poor live in one belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal, so further gains depend on productive jobs in these states.
GS1 · Regional disparity / GS3 · Inclusive growth
With poverty concentrated geographically, the next phase of poverty reduction is a question of regional, job-rich growth.
Jobs grew, earnings did not: employment rose by 13.4 crore (2017-2023), led by rural women entering paid work, but real earnings stayed flat and jobs were in low-productivity activities.
GS3 · Employment
Employment growth without real wage growth signals a quantity-quality gap in India's labour market.
Inequality looks lower but may be understated: the consumption Gini fell to 23.0, yet the Bank warns surveys may miss richer households, and the top 10% earn about 13 times the bottom 10%.
GS2 · Poverty / GS3 · Inequality
Falling consumption inequality coexists with sharp wage inequality; survey design may understate the gap at the top.
Lines and measurement matter: the Bank uses three lines ($3, $4.2, $8.3) in 2021 PPP; new Indian survey data have revised global poverty counts before, so methodology shapes the story.
GS2 · International institutions / GS3 · Measurement
Poverty estimates depend on the line, the PPP base and survey design; India's data revisions shift global counts.
keywords: Converts incomes to a common currency after adjusting for price levels
PPP lines measure what money buys, not its exchange value, so poverty comparisons stay meaningful across countries.
Poverty clustering in a few lagging regions
As poverty concentrates geographically, place-based strategies matter more than nationwide schemes.
Being employed yet earning too little to move up
Jobs concentrated in low-productivity work keep many in working poverty.
Women's rising entry into paid work
The rise of rural women in paid work is driving India's employment growth.
The hardest residual poverty, harder to reduce than the first gains
As headline poverty falls, last-mile poverty needs targeted, region-specific interventions.
Gaps in pay can widen even as gaps in spending narrow
Consumption inequality may fall while earnings inequality stays pronounced.
data: Extreme poverty ($3/day, 2021 PPP), down from 5.3% (2022-23) and 27.1% (2011)
Extreme poverty fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023 (World Bank).
Below the $4.2 line, down from 57.7% in 2011: about 496 million lifted out
About 496 million Indians crossed the $4.2-a-day line between 2011 and 2023 (World Bank).
Share of India's poor living in the belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal
Nearly 57% of India's poor live in the UP–West Bengal belt (World Bank).
Rise in employment, 2017-2023, nearly twice the rise in working-age population; led by rural women
Employment grew by 13.4 crore in 2017-23, driven by rural women entering paid work (World Bank).
Median earnings of the top 10% of workers over the bottom 10%
The top 10% of workers earn about 13 times the bottom 10% (World Bank).
Youth unemployment, Q1 of 2025-26 to Q1 of this fiscal
Youth unemployment rose from 14.6% to 15.9% in a year, even as overall jobs grew.
examples: UP–West Bengal poverty belt
Where most of India's remaining poor live
GS1 · Regional disparity / GS3 · Inclusive growth
The UP–West Bengal belt shows why balanced regional development is now central to poverty reduction.
Women Home Guard aspirants, Jharkhand
About 6,000 women ran trials in Ramgarh for 284 Home Guard posts (Big Picture, page 21)
GS4
GS1 · Women and work
Thousands of rural women racing for a few Home Guard posts show both the aspiration and the scarcity of decent jobs.
pyqs: Poverty and unequal ownership of resources: the 13-times wage gap and concentrated poverty fit here.
Why poverty persists despite schemes: regional concentration and low-productivity jobs are fresh reasons.
Incidence and intensity beyond income: the Bank's multiple lines and non-monetary progress.
Is India's growth inclusive: falling poverty with flat real earnings is a two-sided answer.
Labour-led growth vs productivity: jobs grew in low-productivity activities.

trend.t: GS1 asked why poverty persists (2016, 2018) and how COVID deepened it (2020); GS2 moved to measurement (multidimensional poverty, 2020) and to structural causes such as unequal ownership of resources (2025). GS3 keeps asking whether growth is inclusive (2017, 2019, 2022, 2024, 2025).
trend.watch: Inclusive growth is asked almost every year in GS3, and poverty's structural causes keep returning in GS1 and GS2. Know both the numbers and the reasons poverty persists.
focus: Measuring poverty: lines, PPP and multidimensional indices
Why poverty persists: regions, assets and job quality
Inclusive growth and productive employment
Women's work and household poverty

potential: "Falling poverty in India is increasingly a question of where the poor live and what work they do." Discuss. (15 marks)
India's poverty has declined sharply, yet earnings inequality remains pronounced. Examine the reasons and suggest measures. (10 marks)
Discuss the role of rural women's entry into paid work in India's recent employment growth. What limits its impact on poverty? (10 marks)

practice.q: "Falling poverty in India is increasingly a question of where the poor live and what work they do." Discuss.
parts: Where the poor live: regional concentration
What work they do: jobs and earnings

answer.t: The World Bank estimates India's extreme poverty fell from 27.1% in 2011 to 2.6% in 2023, but about 57% of the remaining poor live in one belt from Uttar Pradesh to West Bengal.

pts.t: Lagging states in the Gangetic plain hold most residual poverty, so national averages hide regional gaps.
pts.ex: The UP–West Bengal belt holds about 57% of the poor.

pts.t: These states have fewer manufacturing and urban jobs to absorb farm labour.
High population growth and young cohorts strain jobs and services.
Small holdings and flood-prone lands keep rural incomes low and volatile.
Lower investment, credit and connectivity limit enterprise.
Weaker delivery of health, education and schemes slows human-capital gains.
Jobs grew by 13.4 crore (2017-23), but mostly in low-productivity activities.
Rural women drove job growth, often in self-employment and unpaid family work.
The top 10% earn about 13 times the bottom 10%.
It rose from 14.6% to 15.9% in a year.
Most workers lack contracts and social security, so shocks push them back into poverty.
Education does not translate into productive jobs.
Industrial corridors, MSME clusters and agro-processing in the eastern belt.
Textiles, food processing and electronics assembly to absorb farm labour.
Apprenticeships linked with employers.
Childcare, safe transport and SHG credit to move women into better-paid work.
Portable benefits under the Code on Social Security.
Regular surveys that capture top incomes and earnings.

answer.t: With the poorest now concentrated in a few regions and in low-paid work, the next fall in poverty will come from productive jobs in the eastern belt, not from transfers alone.

title: Social Security Board for gig workers notified, RSS-linked unions dominate
syllabus: GS3 › Employment; Labour reforms · GS2 › Welfare schemes for vulnerable sections; Statutory bodies · GS1 › Effects of globalisation on society
summary: The Labour Ministry has notified a 40-member National Social Security Board for unorganised, gig and platform workers under the Code on Social Security.
ideas: Closing the social security gap: the board will design, monitor and recommend targeted welfare schemes for unorganised, gig and platform workers, as mandated by the Code on Social Security.
GS3 · Labour reforms
The Code on Social Security for the first time recognises gig and platform workers in law.
Tripartite in form: the board has seven union and seven employer representatives, with the rest from governments and Parliament, and includes aggregators, civil society and platform associations.
GS2 · Statutory bodies
Tripartite boards bring workers, employers and government to one table on welfare design.
Representation matters: the report notes that most of the 12 government-recognised central trade unions are not on the board, raising questions of inclusiveness.
GS2 · Governance / GS3 · Labour
A welfare board's legitimacy depends on how widely it represents workers.
Why it is urgent: platform work is growing while employment, per the World Bank, is concentrated in low-productivity activities with flat real earnings.
GS3 · Employment
Social security for gig work is key when job growth is in low-productivity, informal work.
Who pays and how benefits move: welfare for workers with many platforms needs portable benefits and aggregator contributions.
GS3 · Labour / GS2 · Welfare
Portable, aggregator-funded benefits suit workers who serve many platforms.
keywords: Works through an online platform outside a traditional employer-employee relationship
Platform workers fall outside classic labour law, so they need special social security.
Entitlements that move with the worker across jobs
Portable benefits suit gig workers who switch between platforms.
Workers, employers and government deciding together
Tripartism builds consent for labour welfare policies.
Work allocation and pay set by apps
Algorithmic management makes transparency rights as important as wages for gig workers.
examples: National Social Security Board
40 members for three years, chaired by the Union Labour Minister
GS2 · Statutory bodies / GS3 · Labour
The NSSB shows the Code on Social Security turning into institutions for gig workers.
pyqs: The gig economy and women's empowerment.
The four Labour Codes: merits, demerits and progress.

trend.t: Labour questions moved from globalisation and informalisation (2016) to the gig economy and women (2021) and the four Labour Codes (2024). The thread is the shift from formal jobs to flexible, platform-based work.
trend.watch: Labour Codes and gig work are recent and linked. Expect a question on social security for gig and platform workers under the Code.
focus: Code on Social Security and gig workers
Informality and job quality
Women in the gig economy
Aggregator responsibility and algorithmic management

potential: Discuss the challenges in extending social security to gig and platform workers in India. How does the Code on Social Security address them? (15 marks)

practice.q: Discuss the challenges in extending social security to gig and platform workers in India. How does the Code on Social Security address them?

answer.t: The Labour Ministry has notified a 40-member National Social Security Board for unorganised, gig and platform workers under the Code on Social Security.

pts.t: Platforms call workers 'partners', not employees.
Workers serve several apps, so contributions are hard to assign.
Earnings vary daily.
Many workers stay outside databases.
Opaque pay and deactivation.
Weak unions for dispersed workers.
pts.ex: Most recognised central unions are not on the board.

pts.t: Defines gig and platform workers.
Platforms contribute to a social security fund.
To design and monitor schemes.
Registration of workers for benefits.
Life, disability, health and old-age cover.
Union, employer and government members.
Linked to a universal ID.
Include diverse unions and platform associations.
Rights to know how pay and ratings work.
Learn from state-level gig worker laws.
Insurance and safe-work norms.
Regular surveys of platform work.

answer.t: The Code gives gig workers a legal identity; boards that represent them widely and fund benefits fairly will decide whether it gives them security.

title: 'The opportunity for India is leveraging AI to reimagine how we use machines'
where: Nation, page 14 (Express Rendezvous with Kris Gopalakrishnan); TRAI draft on AI governance, Economy page 23
syllabus: GS3 › Science and technology: developments and their effects; Employment · GS2 › Education and skills; Regulatory bodies · GS4 › Ethics of technology
summary: Infosys co-founder Kris Gopalakrishnan says AI will automate coding and freeze entry-level hiring for now, while TRAI proposes board-level accountability for AI in telecom networks.
ideas: A horizontal technology: like computing, AI affects every sector; its first effect is the 'democratisation of intelligent productivity', starting with software coding, though a human is still needed in the loop.
GS3 · Emerging technology
AI, as a horizontal technology, will reshape every sector, starting with knowledge work like coding.

The entry-level squeeze: IT revenues still grow and there are no mass layoffs, but entry-level hiring is almost zero; graduates without AI skills will struggle, and universities lag three to four years.
GS3 · Employment / GS2 · Education
AI is hitting entry-level jobs first, so curricula must catch up quickly.
India's edge is reskilling at scale: low-cost reskilling keeps margins high, and global capability centres are moving research to India.
GS3 · Industry / Human capital
Reskilling at low cost and global capability centres can turn AI disruption into an Indian advantage.
Products need risk capital: India built services without venture capital; product firms need risk capital and market access, and society needs a bigger appetite for risk.
GS3 · Startups / Investment
India's shift from services to products depends on risk capital and a culture that accepts failure.
Accountability for AI: TRAI's draft asks telecom operators to adopt board-approved AI policies and governance committees and to report AI incidents, staying liable even when AI is outsourced.
GS2 · Regulatory bodies / GS3 · Critical infrastructure
AI governance must keep humans and boards accountable, even when systems are bought from vendors.
keywords: A person checks or approves AI outputs
Keeping a human in the loop preserves accountability in AI-driven decisions.
Multinationals' in-house tech and research hubs
The growth of GCCs shows India moving up from outsourcing to research.
AI performance degrading as data change over time
TRAI flags model drift as a risk when AI runs critical networks.
Inputs designed to fool an AI system
Adversarial attacks on AI can threaten critical infrastructure.
Near-zero entry-level IT hiring is a warning of AI-led jobless growth.
data: Employed by the IT industry, out of a population of 1.4-1.5 billion
IT employs about six million people: a high-income niche, not a mass employer.
examples: TRAI's draft AI framework for telecom
Board-approved AI policies, governance committees, incident reporting
GS4
GS2 · Regulation / GS4 · Accountability
TRAI's draft shows regulators making boards answerable for AI failures.
Binance hack
About $6.3 billion stolen in some 20 minutes via a compromised engineer's laptop (Explained, page 20)
GS3 · Cyber security
The Binance hack shows how one compromised device can expose a whole financial system.
pyqs: Agentic AI: applications, risks and challenges.
Demographic dividend and falling employability: where will jobs come from?
Startups, innovation and employment, and their challenges.
AI as an input for administrative decision-making: an ethical view.

Why is board-level accountability necessary for the use of AI in critical infrastructure such as telecom? (10 marks)

title: 'Can take on grenade, what about idle youths?': Punjab Police despair in border areas
where: Front page anchor, continued on page 2 (Man Aman Singh Chhina)
syllabus: GS3 › Linkages between organised crime and terrorism; Role of external state and non-state actors; Security challenges in border areas · GS2 › India and its neighbourhood; Indian diaspora · GS1 › Youth and unemployment · GS4 › Probity, courage
summary: In Punjab's border districts, gangs with handlers abroad have killed policemen and sarpanchs this year; officers say idle youth drawn to gangs is the deeper problem. (Linked to today's card on Punjab's drug crisis.)
ideas: Crime, terror and handlers abroad: 10–15 gangs operate in Punjab with leaders abroad, in extortion and drugs, reportedly backed by Pakistan's ISI; gangs post videos claiming killings, and an ISI-linked outfit keeps surfacing.
GS3 · Organised crime–terror nexus
Punjab's gangs fuse extortion, drugs and cross-border backing, a textbook crime–terror nexus.

Local officials as targets: since February, six attacks on police personnel have killed five, and sarpanchs and their relatives are being killed; exposed posts, some without boundary walls, show a thinly protected front line.
GS3 · Border area policing
Attacks on police posts and village heads show how border-area governance itself has become a target.
Idle youth, the deeper problem: officers say it is a socio-economic challenge, as young people seek 'work' from gangs, gangsters build social media followings, and quick bail weakens deterrence.
GS1 youth · GS3 internal security
Unemployed youth in border districts become recruits for gangs, making jobs a security issue.
Crime money in politics: the Gurdaspur MP warns of extortion and drug money entering elections through gangsters' relatives and has sought ED and Income Tax probes.
GS2 · Criminalisation of politics
Crime money entering elections threatens the integrity of democracy in border states.
Beyond policing: police offer rewards for information, and a senior officer suggests reserving 1–2% of vacancies in the Army, police and central forces for border youth.
GS3 · Border area development
Employment and community trust are as vital to border security as policing.
keywords: Criminal gangs and terror networks working together
The crime–terror nexus in Punjab blurs the line between gang violence and terrorism.
A hostile state acting through local criminals
Pakistan-backed gangs show proxy violence through local criminals.
Gang leaders directing operations from abroad
Diaspora-based handlers make Punjab's gang problem transnational.
Quick bail weakening the fear of punishment
A deterrence deficit lets hired shooters return to crime within months.
Crime money and criminals entering the electoral process
Gang money in elections deepens the criminalisation of politics.
Earning local trust to deny support to criminals and militants
Jobs and trust deny gangs local support, the core of winning hearts and minds.
examples: Recruitment quota for border youth
A senior officer proposes 1–2% of Army, police and central force vacancies for youth from border areas
GS3 · Border area development
Reserving security-force jobs for border youth turns potential gang recruits into stakeholders in security.
Exposed police posts in border districts
Posts with no boundary walls and few personnel face grenade and gun attacks
GS3 · Border management
Punjab's exposed border posts show why border management needs infrastructure, not just manpower.
Idle youth seeking 'work' from gangs
Officers say young people with time on their hands turn to gangs
GS1 · Consequences of unemployment
In Punjab's border districts, unemployment pushes youth into gangs, showing joblessness as a security risk.
Pakistan-backed gangs and narco-terror networks
Gangs reportedly backed by the ISI; a Pakistan-based gangster is a growing name in cross-border narco-terror
GS2 · India–Pakistan relations
Pakistan's backing of gangs in Punjab shows proxy war as a continuing hurdle in India–Pakistan relations.
Gang leaders abroad
10–15 gangs run by leaders based in the US, UK, Canada and other countries
GS2 · Indian diaspora
Gang networks run from abroad show the misuse of diaspora networks and the need for cooperation with host countries.
pyqs: Linkages between terrorists and organised crime: Punjab's ISI-backed gangs are the live case.
External state and non-state actors: Pakistan-backed gangs and handlers abroad.
Denying local support in border areas: jobs and trust for border youth.

trend.t: Border and security questions moved from managing local perception in border areas (2020) to the challenges of external state and non-state actors (2021) and the crime–terror nexus (2022), and then to border-wide challenges with China and Pakistan (2024) and development-led approaches such as BADP in Ladakh (2026).
trend.watch: Security with a people angle recurs: winning local support (2020) and border area development (2026). The crime–terror nexus and external actors are must-study areas.
focus: Organised crime–terror nexus and narco-terrorism
External state and non-state actors, including diaspora-based handlers
Border area development and youth employment
Criminalisation of politics in border states

Explain the linkages between organised crime and terrorism in India's border states, with examples. (10 marks)

pts.ex: Attacks on police and sarpanchs in Punjab's border districts.

pts.t: Gangs merge with terror and narco networks backed by hostile states.
Handlers hire local youth cheaply through social media.
Extortion and drug money flows across borders.
Host countries' reluctance to act strains bilateral ties.
Crime money enters elections through gangsters' relatives.
Extradition treaties, mutual legal assistance and intelligence sharing with host countries.
Financial investigation of extortion and drug proceeds.

title: The missing middle in India's growth story
syllabus: GS3 › Growth, development and employment; Inclusive growth; Infrastructure; Energy · GS1 › Effects of globalisation; Social stratification
summary: India has stayed lower-middle income for 19 years while Vietnam and China moved up fast; five statistics show jobs, factories, private investment, power and a thin middle class holding it back.
evolution: India enters the World Bank's lower-middle-income group.
Vietnam, lower-middle income since 2009, moves up to upper-middle income this year: about 16 years.
China moves from lower-middle to upper-middle income in 13 years.
India still lower-middle income, 19 years on; five countries move up this year.
ideas: Stuck in the middle: India has been lower-middle income for 19 years; Vietnam and China moved up in 16 and 13. At 8.5% dollar growth, against 5.4% in the past decade, India could get there in about six years.
GS3 · Growth / middle-income trap
Nineteen years after turning lower-middle income, India is still there, while Vietnam took 16 years and China 13 to move up.

Jobs without productivity: the labour force grew by 100 million in under a decade, two-thirds of it women, mostly self-employed in farming; 43% still work in agriculture and 79% of non-farm workers are in informal firms.
GS3 employment · GS1 women
Employment is not productive employment: 43% of India's workers remain in agriculture and 79% of non-farm workers in informal enterprises.

Factories but no factory jobs: registered factories doubled, yet manufacturing's share of output and jobs has not risen; more workers joined the gig economy than formal manufacturing, and capital-intensive growth widened inequality.
GS3 · Manufacturing / inequality
Though registered factories doubled to 2.6 lakh, manufacturing has not become India's ladder of mass upward mobility.
Public investment has not crowded in private investment: infrastructure cut logistics costs, but firms repaired balance sheets and rewarded shareholders instead of investing.
GS3 · Investment
Public infrastructure spending was meant to crowd in private investment, but the private sector has not taken the baton.
Power is a binding constraint: solar has outrun storage and transmission, so output was curtailed even as demand peaked, hurting factories, data centres and AI.
GS3 · Energy / infrastructure
Solar generation running ahead of storage and transmission makes electricity a constraint on India's manufacturing and AI ambitions.
Rich faster than a middle class: 9.4 lakh dollar millionaires, but a broad middle class is not forming; premiumisation and capital outflows follow.
GS3 inclusive growth · GS1 inequality
India is producing millionaires faster than a broad middle class, the missing middle of its growth story.
keywords: Countries stuck at middle income, unable to move up
Without productive jobs, India risks a middle-income trap.
Workers moving from farms to factories and modern services
India's structural transformation has stalled: workers left farms for informal work, not factories.
Jobs with rising output and income per worker
Being employed is not the same as being productively employed.
Work that adds little output, taken because unemployment is unaffordable
The poor cannot afford to be unemployed, so low unemployment hides underemployment.
Public investment drawing in private investment
Public capex has not crowded in private investment.
Growth driven by machines more than labour
Capital-intensive manufacturing has raised profits faster than wages.
Premiumisation reflects growth concentrated at the top.
Women forming a growing share of farm work
Two-thirds of new workers are women, mostly self-employed in farming.
data: Rise in India's labour force in less than a decade; two-thirds women
India's labour force grew by over 100 million in under a decade, two-thirds of it women (World Bank).
Workforce still in agriculture / non-farm workers in informal enterprises
43% of India's workers are in agriculture, and 79% of non-farm workers are in informal enterprises.
Registered factories doubled from 1.3 lakh to 2.6 lakh, yet manufacturing's share stayed flat.
examples: Vietnam
Lower-middle income in 2009; moved up to upper-middle income this year, about 16 years later
Best practice: export-led manufacturing
Vietnam moved from lower- to upper-middle income in 16 years, a model of manufacturing-led growth.
China
Upper-middle income in 2010, 13 years after becoming lower-middle
Best practice: factory-led mobility
China reached upper-middle income in just 13 years by putting workers on factory floors.
Solar curtailment, summer 2026
Solar output cut despite peak demand, for lack of storage and transmission
Energy constraint
In summer 2026, India curtailed solar power even at peak demand for lack of storage and grid.
pyqs: India skipped the manufacturing stage; the missing middle is the result.
Jobs grew with the labour force, but not productive jobs.
Manufacturing failed to become labour-intensive: factories doubled, factory jobs did not.
Industrial growth lagging GDP: manufacturing's share has not risen.
Growth led by more labour, not productivity: the 100 million new workers are mostly in low-value work.
Manufacturing's share in GDP and MSMEs: the core of the missing middle.
Infrastructure investment has cut logistics costs but not yet crowded in private investment.

trend.t: UPSC has asked the same structural question for a decade: India moved from agriculture to services and skipped manufacturing (2014), growth has been jobless (2015), manufacturing failed to become labour-intensive (2017) and growth rests on more labour, not productivity (2022). The latest questions ask for solutions: manufacturing and MSMEs (2023) and labour codes (2024).
trend.watch: Manufacturing and productive employment have come in 2014, 2017 (twice), 2022 and 2023. Structural transformation is a must-study area in GS3.
focus: Manufacturing-led jobs: PLI, MSMEs, labour-intensive sectors
Crowding in private investment after public capex
Power, storage and transmission as constraints on industry
Inequality and the middle class; women's productive employment

potential: India has remained a lower-middle-income country for nearly two decades. Discuss the structural constraints on its growth and suggest a strategy to create high-productivity jobs at scale. (15 marks)
Why has manufacturing not become the engine of employment in India despite the rise in registered factories? Examine. (10 marks)

practice.q: India has remained a lower-middle-income country for nearly two decades. Discuss the structural constraints on its growth and suggest a strategy to create high-productivity jobs at scale.
parts: Introduction: India's 19 years at lower-middle income vs Vietnam and China (one line, with facts)
Strategy for high-productivity jobs (way forward, its own part)

answer.t: India has been lower-middle income since 2007, while Vietnam moved up in 16 years and China in 13 (World Bank).

pts.t: Workers moved from farms into informal work, not factories.
pts.ex: 43% still in agriculture; 79% of non-farm workers informal.

pts.t: Factories doubled, but manufacturing's share of output and jobs has not risen.
pts.ex: 1.3 lakh to 2.6 lakh registered factories, 2004-05 to 2024-25.

pts.t: Machines over labour keep wages behind profits and raise inequality.
Firms deleveraged and paid shareholders instead of building capacity, despite public capex.
Solar outruns storage and transmission, so supply is unreliable.
Two-thirds of new workers are women, mostly self-employed in agriculture.
Many workers lack skills for modern manufacturing and services.
Wealth concentrates at the top, limiting broad-based demand.
Prioritise textiles, apparel, footwear, electronics assembly and food processing.
Tie incentives to employment, not just output.
Credit, technology and easier compliance.
Predictable policy, faster clearances and demand certainty.
Storage, transmission and reliable, affordable supply.
Vocational training, childcare and safe transport to bring women into factories.
Flexibility for firms with social security for workers.

answer.t: India can escape the middle-income trap only by moving its workers from low- to high-productivity jobs, with public infrastructure and private capital working together.

title: Workforce shake-up is here to stay. Brace for it
where: The Editorial Page, page 10; also Explained, page 12 (Soumyarendra Barik)
syllabus: GS3 › Indian economy: employment; Effects of science and technology (AI) on everyday life · GS1 › Population and associated issues · GS4 › Work culture; Ethical concerns in private institutions
summary: The Indian Express argues that AI-led layoffs, like Microsoft's exit offer to 60,000 staff, will hit Indian IT and should make policymakers rethink job strategy for a young India.
evolution: July 2026
Microsoft offers a voluntary retirement programme to over 8,700 staff; over 30% accept, and it then fires 4,800 more (as the editorial notes).
Barclays, HSBC, Oracle, Meta and Amazon are reported to have shed significant parts of their workforce, even as profits grow.
Microsoft's voluntary exit offer to about 60,000 employees, 27% of its workforce, including India (filed on 27 Oct).
The Indian Express editorial: the shake-up is structural, and India's policymakers must prepare.
ideas: AI lets firms do more with fewer people and frees money for AI infrastructure, so layoffs now come even when profits rise.
GS3 · Technology and jobs
AI-led restructuring is cutting jobs even in profitable firms, as Microsoft's 2026 exit offer to 60,000 staff shows.
Indian IT, the largest provider of white-collar jobs, may gain some AI work in the short term but faces headwinds over the medium term.
GS3 · IT sector / services
AI threatens the IT sector, India's largest white-collar employer, more in the medium term than the short term.
The timing is the danger: a youth bulge, too few quality jobs and growing unrest among the young.
GS1 demography · GS3 employment
AI's labour-replacing power arrives just as India's youth bulge needs quality jobs, risking a demographic burden instead of a dividend.
AI can affect everyone: TCS's cut of about 12,000 jobs (2025) fell mainly on middle and senior managers, not just juniors.
GS3 employment · GS4 work culture
AI-led restructuring spares no level: TCS's 2025 cuts fell mainly on middle and senior managers.
The diaspora angle: Indian engineers in the US on H-1B visas must find a new sponsor within about 60 days of losing their job, or leave.
GS2 · Indian diaspora
AI-led layoffs hit the Indian diaspora hard: H-1B workers have about 60 days to find a new sponsor or leave the US.
Technological disruption is also an ethical question of work culture: how firms treat people they no longer need, and the job insecurity and stress that follow.
GS4 · Work culture
An ethical work culture treats layoffs with transparency, fair compensation and support, not pressure to 'choose' an exit.
keywords: Job losses or hiring freezes as AI takes over tasks
